name: Jamaica Plain
headline: A kettle pond, an arboretum and a cemetery park,
with the Orange Line running under a linear park.
answer: Jamaica Plain is a Boston neighborhood of 4.4 square miles between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, part of the town of West Roxbury until it was annexed to Boston in 1874. Its housing runs from triple-deckers built from the 1870s onward to Victorian houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 41,012 people there in 2020. Four Orange Line stations run under the Southwest Corridor Park, and the Needham Line stops at Forest Hills.
meta: Jamaica Plain, Boston: triple-deckers and Victorian houses between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, with four Orange Line stops and the Needham Line.

boundaries.text: Jamaica Plain lies south of Roxbury's Jackson and Egleston Squares, with the Jamaicaway, Olmsted Park and Jamaica Pond on its western side, Franklin Park to the east, and the Arnold Arboretum and Forest Hills at its southern end.

overview: Families settled south of Parker Hill in 1630, shortly after Boston and Roxbury were founded, and the name Jamaica appears on maps by the late 1650s. In 1676 John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas gave land for the community's first school, later the Eliot School. For most of a century from 1795, the Jamaica Pond Aqueduct Corporation piped water from the pond to Boston and Roxbury. The Boston and Providence Rail Road arrived in 1834, and in 1851 estate owners here helped split from Roxbury to form the town of West Roxbury, which voted to join Boston in 1873; annexation took effect in 1874. Breweries opened too: Highland Spring on Heath Street from 1867 and Haffenreffer, near Boylston and Amory Streets, from 1871 until 1964.

Triple-deckers first appeared in the 1870s and spread quickly in the 1890s. Larger houses went up on former estates: Sumner Hill on the Greenough land, Parley Vale and Robinwood Avenue in the 1880s, and Moss Hill and Woodland Road on Bowditch family land in the 1890s. By the early 20th century most buildable lots were filled. Much of the neighborhood's edge is parkland: four of the eight parks in Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace (Olmsted Park, Jamaica Pond, the Arnold Arboretum and the Arborway) run along its western and southern sides, Franklin Park borders it to the east, and the 1848 Forest Hills Cemetery sits at its southern tip.

In 1969 Governor Francis Sargent cancelled a planned extension of I-95 through the area after community opposition. The cleared land became the Southwest Corridor: the Orange Line moved from the elevated Washington Street line into a below-grade cut in May 1987, and the park above it was completed in 1990. On March 2, 2017, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: JP/ROX, guidelines for about 250 acres between Forest Hills, Egleston Square and Jackson Square, generally bounded by Washington Street, Columbus Avenue and Amory Street, covering housing, jobs, urban design and transportation.

housing.text: Jamaica Plain's housing mixes wood-frame triple-deckers, built from the 1870s and especially in the 1890s, with late-19th-century single-family houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill and Moss Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 18,129 occupied housing units in the neighborhood, 45.6% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: The Monument and Centre Street
areas.line: The intersection of Centre and South Streets, marked by the Soldiers' Monument, is the neighborhood's traditional center; the 1760 Loring-Greenough House stands on the square at 12 South Street.

areas.name: Hyde Square
areas.line: The area around Centre, Day and Perkins Streets, extending east along Centre Street toward Jackson Square.

areas.name: Jackson Square and Egleston Square
areas.line: Squares at the northern edge, on Columbus Avenue and Washington Street at the Roxbury line; Jackson Square has an Orange Line station, and both fall within the PLAN: JP/ROX study area.

areas.name: Forest Hills
areas.line: The southern end around the Arborway, Morton, Walk Hill and South Streets, with Forest Hills Cemetery and the Forest Hills station, rebuilt in 1987 for the Orange Line and commuter rail.

stations: Heath Street (terminus, at the neighborhood's northern edge)

commute.text: The Orange Line runs below street level through Jamaica Plain to Back Bay and downtown, and Forest Hills station, at Washington Street and Hyde Park Avenue, is also a Needham Line commuter rail stop and the terminal for 16 MBTA bus routes. The Green Line E branch ends at Heath Street, and the 39 bus is the neighborhood's main bus route. The Southwest Corridor Park carries a bike path beside the Orange Line, and the Jamaicaway and Arborway run along the Emerald Necklace.

places.name: Jamaica Pond
places.line: A spring-fed glacial kettle hole more than 50 feet deep, taken into the park system in 1891, with a boathouse and bandstand from 1912 and seasonal boat rentals; a 1.5-mile path circles it.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum
places.line: A 281-acre preserve founded in 1872 and part of the Emerald Necklace, open free every day.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, White Stadium and the William J. Devine Golf Course; it connects Jamaica Plain with Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Roslindale.

places.name: Forest Hills Cemetery
places.line: A garden cemetery founded in 1848 as Roxbury's municipal cemetery and designed by Henry A. S. Dearborn, entered from Morton Street; it was added to the National Register in 2004.

places.name: Loring-Greenough House
places.line: A 1760 country house at 12 South Street, owned since 1924 by the Jamaica Plain Tuesday Club and designated a Boston Landmark in 1999.

places.name: Southwest Corridor Park
places.line: A linear park managed by DCR from Back Bay station to Forest Hills, built over the Orange Line on land cleared for a cancelled highway; its first segments opened in 1987.

places.name: Haffenreffer Brewery buildings
places.line: The former Haffenreffer brewery, which brewed from 1871 until 1964, now houses the Boston Beer Company's Samuel Adams brewery.

history.text: John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas donated land for the community's first school, later named the Eliot School.
Jamaica Plain became part of the new town of West Roxbury, set off from Roxbury.
Annexation to Boston took effect after West Roxbury voters approved it in 1873.
The rebuilt Forest Hills station opened on May 4, and Orange Line trains began running through the Southwest Corridor on May 7, replacing the elevated line on Washington Street.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Jamaica Plain?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists Jamaica Plain on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $1,256,250, across 69 sales. In 2024 it was $1,157,500, across 64 sales. Condominium figures for Jamaica Plain could not be read from the table.

faq.q: Does Jamaica Plain have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. The Needham Line stops at Forest Hills, which is also the southern terminal of the Orange Line. The Orange Line has three more Jamaica Plain stations: Green Street, Stony Brook and Jackson Square.

faq.q: Which school district serves Jamaica Plain?
faq.a: Boston Public Schools. School assignment is set by the district; review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: Which parks are in or next to Jamaica Plain?
faq.a: Jamaica Pond, Olmsted Park, the Arnold Arboretum and the Arborway, all part of the Emerald Necklace, run along its western and southern sides, and Franklin Park, Boston's largest open space at 485 acres, borders it to the east.

notes: Written 2026-10-22. Population: Boston Planning & Development Agency Research Division, 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods, 2020 Decennial Census Redistricting Data and 2016-2020 American Community Survey' (April 2022), table 'Population by Age Group', total 41,012. This is a neighborhood figure (BPDA approximates neighborhoods with 2020 census block groups), not a planning-district figure; I did not find a planning-district table. The same agency's 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods' (estimates as of January 1, 2025, https://bostonplans.org/documents/research/population-and-demographics/2025/boston-in-context-2025, approximated with census tracts) gives 42,949; not used because the schema field is 2020. Housing tenure is from the 2022 report's Housing Tenure table (ACS 2016-2020, B25003/B25001); the triple-decker and estate dates in the housing text are from Wikipedia's Jamaica Plain article. Market: Warren Group single-family row read twice in this session with identical YTD figures; condo table truncated at Brookline in both fetches, so condo fields are null. The 4.4 square miles, settlement, Eliot School, aqueduct, brewery and sub-area facts are from Wikipedia. Conflicts left out: Wikipedia's Jamaica Plain article gives Franklin Park as 527 acres and Jamaica Pond as about 60 acres, while the City of Boston gives Franklin Park as 485 acres and the Jamaica Pond article gives 68 acres; the city figure is used for Franklin Park and the pond's acreage is omitted. Forest Hills Cemetery acreage is given as both 275 and 250 acres on Wikipedia, so it is omitted. Southwest Corridor Park length is given as both 4.1 and 4.7 miles, so it is omitted. Forest Hills station is also served by some Providence/Stoughton and Franklin/Foxboro trains per Wikipedia; only the Needham Line (confirmed on the MBTA timetable, https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Needham/timetable) is listed. The MBTA stop page (https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-forhl) confirms the Washington St and Hyde Park Ave address. The Soldiers' Monument is named from Wikipedia; its date was not confirmed. No historic district designations were confirmed for Jamaica Plain. Schools: assignment is by address and set by Boston Public Schools; no school is named. Nearby: Roxbury and Roslindale border Jamaica Plain but are not in the current neighborhood slug list. Fair housing: Wikipedia's account of the 1970s and 1980s describes redlining and who moved in as rents fell; that people-focused history was left out, and only the highway cancellation and the transit and park outcomes are described.
